But these questions were not raised by cranks or shock jocks , nor by militants for some malevolent cause . They were raised by scholars , scientists and writers , most of whom were unprepared for what hit them . They were not just criticised , as advocates of any strong position ought to be , but censored , punished , fired , threatened , harassed , demonised , libelled , and in some cases physically assaulted . <h> Threat to freedom of speech <p> Freedom of speech is protected in all democracies . Yet the repression of controversial ideas is no longer a hallmark @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the very institutions most committed to exploring ideas . <p> The ever-present threat to freedom of speech emerges from two features of our psychology . One is that people hold many factual beliefs not because the beliefs have been shown to be true but because they are felt to uphold a moral order . The other is that upholding a moral order takes place in the arena of common knowledge . <p> First , a few words on why academic freedom should matter . Societies entrust universities , at fantastic expense , with a mandate to discover and transmit knowledge . This can not be accomplished without intellectual freedom . No one is infallible or omniscient . Mortal humans begin in ignorance and are saddled with cognitive biases that make the search for knowledge arduous . The only way our species has managed to learn anything is by a process of conjecture and refutation . Some venture ideas , others probe whether they are sound , and in the long run the better ideas prevail . <p> I 'm focusing on the drive by academics to censor one another @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ values of a university in a liberal democracy . Why does repressing speech come so naturally to people that it bleeds through even in institutions dedicated to the exchange of ideas ? <p> Why do people cancel ? Lurking beneath each of the cancellable ideas with which I began <p> this column , one can find a laudable moral principle . Racism , sexism , homophobia , transphobia and Islamophobia are evils which must be combatted . Rape is a heinous crime . Climate change is a serious problem that will cause severe damage unless mitigated . <p> Canadian cognitive psychologist Steven Pinker <p> Matt Writtle <h> No such thing as a fact <p> Universities aim to develop objective knowledge about big questions . But academics are only human , and despite their training in making conceptual distinctions , they are apt to avow whichever factual claims make their moral positions more compelling . Sexual discrimination and harassment are wrong , and anyway men and women are exactly the same . Rape is a vicious crime , and also men have no natural inclination to do it . War is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ never waged it . <p> The repression of controversial ideas is no longer a hallmark of dictatorships but increasingly a fixture of universities <p> Worse , many scholars blow off the distinction between facts and values not despite their academic training but because of it . The postmodern current in the humanities explicitly denies that there is any such thing as truth , fact , or objectivity , insisting all such claims are pretexts to power . And in defiance of their universities ' mission statements , many academics believe that the primary purpose of a university is not to discover and transmit knowledge but to pursue social justice , conceived as the wresting of power by victim groups from oppressor groups . <p> So it 's easy to blur the pursuit of objective knowledge with the upholding of moral norms , even in academia , especially in the sectors of academia that never signed on to the ideal of objective knowledge in the first place . What terrifies the censors and cancellers , it appears , is not that a dangerous idea might be thought , but that it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ case can be made for keeping a small number of particularly dangerous questions out of common knowledge , the default clearly must be intellectual freedom . <p> This is an edited extract from When Everyone Knows That Everyone Knows by Steven Pinker ( Allen Lane , ? 13.99 ) . @@130458022 <h> There are parts of the world in which people wo n't be able to cool by sweating if this trajectory continues . <p> Conditions are on course to become unliveable in certain areas ( Image : Getty ) <p> Those claiming that concerns over climate change are rooted in hysteria are badly mistaken and unfortunately not restricted to the non-scientific community . The recent article by Craig Walton claiming that the risks of climate change have been exaggerated was unfortunately based on false claims . For instance , Dr Walton , who studies the origins of planets , wrote : " Claims of increasing frequency and danger of extreme weather events broadly lack strong scientific backing " . <p> This is simply untrue . The most recent assessment by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change , which reviewed the scientific literature , concluded : " Human-induced climate change is already affecting many weather and climate extremes in every region across the globe . Evidence of observed changes in extremes such as heatwaves , heavy precipitation , droughts , and tropical cyclones , and , in particular , their attribution @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this week , the Met Office published evidence that severe heatwaves and droughts are making extreme wildfires more frequent and intense worldwide . <p> Readers could forgiven for thinking Dr Walton dismissed as claims that climate change could threaten human civilisation , but his talk of " misinformation " was a statement of hope rather than knowledge . The truth is we do not know how human societies will cope with the climate we are creating . <p> The most recent analysis by the United Nations Environment Programme of countries policies and plans for tackling climate change concluded that global average temperature could be nearly 3 Celsius degrees higher by the end of this century compared with the period before the Industrial Revolution , when we started releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels . <p> The Earth has not experienced such a global average temperature since the Pliocene Epoch about 3 million years , when the polar ice caps were much smaller than today and sea level was 5 to 25 metres higher than today . <p> Article continues belowADVERTISEMENT <p> As human civilisation was created @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ appeared less than 250,000 years ago , Dr Walton assertions that we could cope with such a climate is little more than wishful thinking . <p> We should not be complacent about the risks that climate change is creating . Global average temperature is already about 1.4 Celsius degrees higher than before the Industrial Revolution , and the UK is suffering from more intense summer heatwaves and winter rainfall . This summer was the warmest on record , even warmer than the summer of 2022 when unprecedented temperatures of more than 40 degrees Celsius occurred for the first time in many parts of the country . <p> In some parts of the world , daytime temperature and humidity are now approaching levels at which it will be dangerous for people to be outside because they will not be able to cool down by sweating . As global temperature rises , these parts of the world could become difficult to inhabit . <p> There is no doubt that the impacts of climate change are increasing and harming lives and livelihoods around the world . These impacts will only stop worsening when @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Complacency or denial about these risks will only lead to more suffering . <p> There is no logical reason why any politician or scientist should reject the scientific evidence for climate change . Instead they should be leading public and policy debates about the best ways of tackling greenhouse gas emissions , and making our societies more resilient against those impacts of climate change that can not now be avoided . <p> Bob Ward is the Policy and Communications Director at the Grantham Institute <h> Read next <p> Invalid email <p> We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you 've consented to and to improve our understanding of you . This resilience partly reflected a frontloading of demand in anticipation of tariffs , which temporarily boosted activity but is unlikely to be sustained . As this effect fades , global growth dynamics are expected to soften further . <p> A predictable and open international economic order remains essential to sustain global trade , investment and shared prosperity . While recent preliminary trade agreements have reduced uncertainty , it remains elevated and may weigh on investment . We are determined to ensure that inflation stabilises at our 2% target in the medium term . We will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance and are not pre-committing to a particular rate path . In particular , our interest rate decisions will be based on the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it , as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission . Stronger growth in the first quarter partly reflected a frontloading of trade ahead of expected tariff increases , which reversed in the second quarter . <p> Higher tariffs , a stronger euro and increased global competition are expected to hold back growth for the rest of the year , but the effect of these headwinds on growth should fade next year . Surveys point to robust growth in services , indicating some positive underlying momentum in the economy . Furthermore , despite some signs of softening labour demand , the labour market remains resilient . This should support consumer spending over time . Consumer spending and investment should both benefit from more favourable financing conditions as our interest rate cuts feed through to the economy . Increased government spending on infrastructure and defence should also support investment . This is reflected in the latest ECB staff projections , which foresee growth of 1.2% in 2025 , 1.0% in 2026 and 1.3% in 2027 . <p> Risks to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tariff-related downside risks materialising has fallen , owing to the new trade deal . At the same time , the risk remains that renewed trade tensions could further dampen exports , investment and consumption . Geopolitical tensions remain a major source of uncertainty . In contrast , higher than expected defence and infrastructure spending in the EU , together with productivity-enhancing reforms , would add to growth . By fostering innovation , diversification and resilience , such ambitious reforms would also mitigate the economic tail risks arising from geopolitical tensions . <p> In the current environment , governments should address the considerable need for strategic investment while ensuring sustainable public finances . Where more efficient spending leads to higher growth , this would also create fiscal space , providing room for greater public investment in strategically important areas . <p> Strengthening the euro area 's resilience and competitiveness is crucial in this environment . " <p> Riccardo Arosi @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " Thanks to the high resolution of the new bathymetric database -- 500 metres per pixel compared to the 1 -- 2 kilometres per pixel of previous maps -- we could apply semi-automated techniques more reliably to identify , profile and analyse submarine canyons , " said Riccardo Arosio , of the Marine Geosciences Research Group at University College Cork . <p> The researchers also developed GIS software script that allows them " to calculate a wide range of canyon-specific morphometric parameters in just a few clicks " . <h> What do these canyons look like ? <p> Not all the canyons are the same depending on their location on the continent . <p> The canyons in the east are described as having " a more complex and branched , often forming extensive canyon -- channel systems with typical U-shaped cross section , " then in contrast , the ones in the west are " shorter and steeper , characterized by V-shaped cross sections . @@130558900 <p> We 're going dark . The Earth is reflecting less light than it used to , especially the Northern Hemisphere . While climate change is to blame , the reverse is also true : the planet being darker -- and absorbing light instead of reflecting it -- is in turn worsening climate change . But scientists are still unsure exactly how the change in Earth 's reflectivity will affect our planet 's future . <h> A light problem <p> Climate change is darkening the Earth , according to a study published in the journal PNAS . Data from NASA 's Clouds and the Earth 's Radiant Energy System ( CERES ) satellites found that the planet is reflecting much less light into space than it did two decades ago . In addition , while both sides of the planet should be receiving and reflecting equal amounts of sunlight , Earth 's Northern Hemisphere ( NH ) is reflecting less than the Southern Hemisphere ( SH ) , thus retaining more heat and appearing dimmer . <p> This affects the Earth 's radiation budget , which is the " amount @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ outgoing longwave radiation , " said Popular Mechanics . Any imbalance between the NH and SH is typically " offset by the oceanic currents that transport energy from the southern hemisphere to the northern hemisphere . " But this research suggests that " surface changes have tipped the balance so much that ocean currents have n't been making up the difference for the past two decades . " <p> Along with the NH dimming and warming more than the SH , the " NH tropics are getting wetter , which suggests changes in large-scale atmospheric circulation are occurring , " said the study . <h> A dim future <p> The reason for this phenomenon , like most environmental problems , is climate change . Melting Arctic ice and reduced snow cover are actively dimming the glow of the planet . The NH " used to be so snowy that all that white was bouncing tons of light back into space , " said Vice . Temperatures have increased , melting the snow cover and " exposing these darker surfaces that absorb more sunlight instead of reflecting it , " said @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ contributed to the dimming Earth . Low-lying clouds " decreased in recent decades , " said Popular Mechanics . Ironically , this may be because we have been polluting less than we used to . In the NH , " stricter environmental regulations have reduced aerosol pollution , which previously reflected sunlight , " said the BBC . So , while the air has been cleaner , it has also incurred an unintended consequence . On the SH , " aerosol levels are increasing due to events like bushfires and volcanic eruptions , which reflect more sunlight . " <p> In a positive feedback loop , the Earth 's darkening is " accelerating the effects of climate change , and an asymmetric hemispheric darkening could produce its own complex impacts , including disruptive shifts in precipitation , " said 404 Media . Researchers are " watching for signs that the symmetry might reemerge in the future , or if asymmetry is perhaps the new normal . @@130584341 <h> Breadcrumb <h> ' Animals matter as we plan our world ' <p> Starling.An adult bird flying to the nest to feed a chick . Image : RSPB <p> RSPB <p> Why animal welfare belongs in planning permission decisions . <p> To treat animal welfare as irrelevant is to deny that the built environment has consequences for animals . <p> Planning permission is often thought of as a technical process : assessments of traffic , design , noise , and environmental impact . But planning is also about values . It decides not just what gets built , but what kind of society we are building . <p> The recent High Court case of Animal Equality UK v North East Lincolnshire Council &amp; ASL New Clee Limited 2025 EWHC 1331 ( Admin ) illustrates this . Although the claim against the UK 's first proposed onshore salmon farm was dismissed , the judgment reaffirmed something vital : animal welfare can be a material planning consideration . <p> This recognition matters because it brings the lives of animals into the heart of decisions that affect their lives . <p> Sentient <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ allowed to take into account when deciding a planning application . It matters because only material considerations can influence whether permission is granted or refused . <p> Some things are always material , like local planning policies , while others material considerations are optional : the council can choose to consider them if relevant . <p> In practice , the planning officer 's report highlights what they think are the key material issues ( like traffic , noise , or ecology ) in the planning application . Councillors can accept or reject that advice , but they must base their decision on material factors . <p> Decisions about farms , zoos , or wildlife facilities are not only about land use , but affect how animals will live . <p> The UK 's Animal Welfare ( Sentience ) Act 2022 acknowledges animals , including fish , as sentient beings and as such a large portion of the public will understandably feel strongly that the potential suffering animals will experience should be relevant to planning decisions . <p> Mortality <p> Just as climate change and air quality have gradually become central @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . What once seemed " beyond planning " could now become integral . <p> Public concern for animal welfare is at an all-time high . Ignoring it risks undermining trust in planning committees as bodies that are meant to respond to the community 's and society 's expectations . <p> Represented by Advocates for Animals and Alex Shattock of Landmark Chambers , Animal Equality UK challenged the approval of a large onshore salmon farm in Cleethorpes . <p> Expert evidence highlighted the severe welfare risks to salmon in intensive tanks , which included disease , injury , cannibalism , and mass mortality . <p> Economic <p> While the council ultimately granted permission , the High Court confirmed that animal welfare is not excluded from planning law and can be a material planning consideration . Committees may take it into account if they choose . <p> This judgment does not mandate consideration of animal welfare by local planning authorities , but it keeps the door wide open for welfare arguments to play a role in future planning battles . <p> This decision has paved the way for similar cases . We @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for an intensive poultry unit , a zoo where welfare had been sidelined and most recently a puppy farm was refused planning permission due to animal welfare concerns . <p> The public mood is shifting toward recognising animals not just as economic units but as living beings deserving proper consideration in decision-making , just like humans . <p> Campaigners <p> With every acknowledgment that welfare is a " material consideration , " the ground moves further toward embedding it in planning culture . <p> Planning is about shaping communities , landscapes , and the conditions of life for humans , the environment and animals alike . To treat animal welfare as irrelevant is to deny that the built environment has consequences for animals . <p> Recognising welfare in planning aligns local decision-making with national values on sentience and gives councillors the discretion , and the responsibility , to act in ways that reflect that . <p> Each time a planning committee acknowledges welfare , each time campaigners raise it as material , and each time the courts affirm its relevance , the principle takes deeper root : that animals matter @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Download <h> NEWSLETTERS <p> Sign up for our WEEKLY newsletters - and never miss out on the amazing news and comment articles we publish . <h> ABOUT US <p> The Ecologist is an environmental news and analysis website with a focus on environmental , social and economic justice . <p> Our aim is to educate and inform as many people as possible about the wonders of nature , the crisis we face and the best solutions and methods in managing that crisis . We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone , paid for by those who can afford it . <p> Your support makes all the difference . <p> AI-generated images of starving children , refugees , victims of armed conflict , and much more , are spreading across the internet . <p> New research from Dr Arsenii Alenichev , at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp , has uncovered a vast collection of pictures and video clips for sale . They appear to depict the struggles of poor and vulnerable people around the world but they are , in fact , the reductive fever dreams of Generative AI . <p> They are clearly marked as AI , so purchasers are not being deceived , but that only makes this trend all the more alarming : there is an emerging market for AI-generated poverty porn . <p> A quick search on stock image websites reveal pictures that are truly shocking . " Asian children " swim in rivers of waste , skeletal infants stare hungrily at the viewer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ encampments . And , of course , there are plenty of white Westerners coming to the rescue . Volunteers in baseball caps embracing grateful African children , picture-perfect 20-somethings pose in schools full of smiling students , and foreign doctors in white coats bring modern medicine to the needy . <p> Some images are just ridiculous . The caption of one reads : " Young mother cradles her child amidst the chaos of war in Africa " , which it advertises as " powerful imagery for awareness campaigns " . The backdrop to this scene of war-torn chaos is , inexplicably , a perfectly intact cafe . <p> We are in the foothills of AI imagery and so we must expect such obvious mistakes will be ironed out quickly . As the pictures become increasingly sophisticated and photorealistic , the difference between the real and the fake will become impossible to discern and the temptation to use them will increase . But can we ever trust AI to make images that are n't laden with stereotypes , and is it ever ethical ? <p> Alenichev 's earlier research exemplifies the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ can be highly racialised and this is particularly visible in the images they create . The models are trained on billions of pictures from our past and present ; imbibing all of our biases and prejudices in the process . <p> In recent years , many NGOs have adopted ethical storytelling guidelines that forbids them from using dehumanising photographs of the people they serve . But in light of extreme funding cuts -- from Keir Starmer 's slashing of the UK aid budget to the almost complete eradication of the United States Agency for International Development ( USAID ) -- many fundraising teams , in charities large and small , are under intense pressure to fill the yawning financial gaps . <p> Meanwhile , the need for effective visual communication has never been greater ; to feed the insatiable social media accounts , websites , fundraising appeals , etc . In these circumstances the use of AI stock images for marketing might prove irresistible . <p> After all , fake photos of fake people are cheap . There are no photographers to contract and no trips to be arranged . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ security risks to manage , no duty of care , no obligations . Nobody is being objectified or exploited , right ? Wrong . @@130630761 <h> Kanchha Sherpa obituary : Part of team that climbed Everest in 1953 <p> Last surviving member of the British expedition that made history dies aged 92 <p> The Times <p> Wednesday October 22 2025 , 5.00pm , The Times <p> Ascending Everest helped Kanchha Sherpa 's family escape poverty <p> The Times <p> Wednesday October 22 2025 , 5.00pm , The Times <p> In 1952 the Swiss made two attempts to climb what was known in the West as Mount Everest , the highest peak in the world . Neither were successful but the mountaineering team caught the eye of a 19-year-old called Kanchha Sherpa as they passed through his home town of Namche , a village in the foothills of the Himalayas . <p> Kanchha was particularly excited to spot Tenzing Norgay , one of the most experienced sherpas -- Himalayan mountain guides -- in the region . He had attempted to climb Everest , known by locals as Chomolungma , six times . " Tenzing was like a king , " Kanchha recalled , " a very important man . " <p> For the rest of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to and from neighbouring Tibet for two to three rupees a day . One day he came across a well-dressed sherpa as he was lugging a basket of potatoes on a trail below Namche . " I asked ' Where did you get the money to buy that jacket ? ' " he recalled . " And he says , ' In Darjeeling , working for Tenzing Norgay ' . " <p> It was an enticing prospect . Kanchha had no great dreams to scale Everest but he was born into poverty and struggled to find work to support his family . Western mountaineers tackled the peak out of personal fulfilment , glory or record-setting , but for Kanchha it was an opportunity to make money . The work , he was told , would pay double what he earned . <p> With two friends , he decided to travel by foot to Tenzing 's home in Darjeeling in early 1953 . It took four days and when they arrived , in the dead of night , Tenzing came to the window and asked for their fathers ' names ; @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trade , primarily between Solukhumbu and Tibet , and Tenzing knew him . He was invited in and his two friends sent back into the cold . <p> For the next few weeks , Tenzing provided Kanchha with new clothes and a bed while Kanchha did chores around the home -- laundry , helping in the kitchen , carrying pales of water . Then he told Kanchha they were heading to Kathmandu , where a group led by Colonel John Hunt , who was on leave from the British Army , had gathered for another attempt to scale the 8,849m ( 29,032ft ) peak . It was the first time Kanchha had met westerners , including the New Zealander Edmund Hillary . " The English , they had round eyes , yellow hair , " Kanchha recalled , " and Hillary -- he was so so tall ! " <p> On March 10 , 1953 , the first party of 35 climbers left the Kathmandu Valley with 150 porters , followed by a second party with 200 porters the next day . It took them 16 days to reach Namche @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . From there only the climbers and local sherpas , supported by yaks , continued on to base camp . <p> Kanchha 's life was transformed by the ascent <p> ROBIC UPADHAYAY/AFP/GETTY IMAGES <p> Kanchha 's job was to carry heavy loads of food , equipment and tents as the team made their way to six camps before the final summit . He had no training but the more experienced sherpas taught him how to walk with crampons and use an ice axe on the mountain face . They survived on roasted corn , canned western food and poor-quality army boots that blistered their feet ; there was no supplemental oxygen . When they came across a vast crevasse en route to the first camp they had to hike back to Namche , cut ten pine trees , carry them up and make a wooden bridge . <p> By the evening of May 21 , Kanchha and 13 other porters were huddled in a tent high on the Lhotse face . Some of the sherpas were too frightened to leave the camp , so Tenzing and Hillary ascended the mountain @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ us tea and gave us some snacks , " recalled Kanchha . " Some sherpas ' feet were cold , and so he rubbed them to warm them up ... Tenzing , he was a very strong man , but also a very kind man for his workers . " <p> The following day Kanchha followed Hillary and Tenzing to the South Col ( the final camp ) to drop off his 60lb load of equipment . He was one of only three sherpas to make it to the final camp but they could not go any further because they did not have permits and they first heard that Tenzing and Hillary had reached the summit on May 29 via a crackly radio . They were finally reunited at camp two . " There was no alcohol , so we celebrated with tea and snacks , " Kanchha recalled . " We danced , hugged and kissed . It was a moment of pure joy . " <p> News of the ascent trickled down to base camp , where a Times journalist named James Morris , later famous as Jan @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the 20th century . The message he typed was coded , so as to not be intercepted by rival newspapers , and handed to sherpas who set out at first light for the British embassy in Kathmandu , where it was sent on to London . On June 2 , 1953 -- the day of Queen Elizabeth II 's coronation -- the front-page story of The Times carried the headline : Everest Conquered . <p> The Times on June 2 , 1953 , with the Everest story top right <p> Kanchha was the last surviving member of the expedition team . Tenzing died in 1986 , Hillary in 2008 . A spiritual man , Kanchha prayed most days for Tenzing and Hillary " because they brought prosperity to the Khumbu , to the sherpas " . The walls of his house in Namche were decorated with old mementos including a note from Hillary and medals from the Queen that Hillary eventually brought back to Namche . <p> Ang Phurba " Kanchha " Sherpa was born in 1933 in Namche Bazaar , the central trading hub of the Khumbu region @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ birth date ) . Though the swell of tourism has since brought locals to relative prosperity , he grew up in poverty . Most sherpas made a living from farming and would forage in the woods for mushrooms and plants to eat . " We had no money and little food , " he said . " Some people had potatoes , but some people had no potatoes . " <p> Kanchha continued working as a sherpa for foreign mountaineers after the 1953 expedition . He made six more trips up the peak ( but did not reach the summit ) before his wife , Ang Lhakpa Sherpa , convinced him to retire in 1973 , weeks after a deadly avalanche . In retirement he joined a trekking company called Mountain Travel Nepal and became something of a local celebrity . He ran a speaking programme for tourists in Namche called " Story Time with Kanchha " and started a foundation in his name to provide educational opportunities and preserve sherpa culture . <p> Kanchha 's wife survives him along with four sons , two daughters and eight grandchildren , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cryosphere analyst and campaigner who studies the impact of climate change on glaciers in the Himalayas and took part in the 2019 National Geographic expedition that installed automatic weather stations high on Everest . <p> Kanchha never minded that he did not reach the summit . It was not a peak to be conquered but rather respected and in later years Kanchha was vocal about the ways in which mountaineering tourism was ravaging his sacred mountain . When he was a boy there were several feet of snow in winter . Now the summits were black . " They should not be dirtying the mountain , " he said . " It is our biggest god . @@130648860 <p> It was a very early morning in August when an entire mountainside in Alaska 's Tracy Arm fjord detached and slid into the deep ocean water beneath it . <p> The slide created a gargantuan splash -- a hyper-local , but massive tsunami that ran up the opposite mountain slope , leveling everything in its path as high as the Empire State Building . It ripped evergreens out of the ground , stripped a nearby island to bare rock and pulverized the glacial ice around it . <p> The whole episode lasted minutes . <p> About 15 miles away , a National Geographic cruise ship carrying around 150 passengers and crew started to move backward , pulled by suddenly shifting currents through an eerie fog . <p> And twenty miles across the fjord 's channel , three sea kayakers camping on high ground woke up to ocean water dripping into their tent , their gear strewn across the shore . One kayak was lost , swirling around in an ocean whirlpool . <p> It would take days for the scale of the split-second devastation to become clear , but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or killed . The National Geographic cruise ship , in particular , was saved by the fact it was positioned behind an S-shaped bend in the fjord that blunted the impact of a wall of water rushing down the channel . <p> " That probably saved their lives , " said Jackie Caplan-Auerbach , a seismologist and professor at Western Washington University , who was in touch with the ship 's captain and relayed the tale to CNN . <p> But scientists who study these types of landslides are anxious it could happen again . Tracy Arm is a popular route for cruise ships packed with ice-chasing tourists eager for a glimpse of Arctic glaciers before they disappear . <p> " I 've looked at the cruise ship schedules , " Caplan-Auerbach said . " On any given day , there are often a couple of cruise vessels with quite literally thousands of people aboard . " <p> High above the cold , clear waters of the Gulf of Alaska , the mountains are moving , inching down toward the water line . <p> All in all , scientists have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ slow-moving landslides " in Alaska . Some are moving literal inches ; others more than 10 feet per year . <p> Some of these mountainsides have dislodged themselves deep in the bedrock , causing the face of a mountain to shear clean off -- as has happened at least twice in the last two years . <p> If such a enormous volume of rock , soil and debris falls into a deep body of water , whether a glacial lake or the ocean , the result is a dangerous tsunami . <p> Many scientists believe this phenomenon is being spurred in part by rapidly melting glaciers exposing the mountainside . Without thick sheets of ice to buttress it , the rock face becomes destabilized . Alaska has warmed 4.5 degrees since 1950 , according to federal data , and is the fastest-warming US state . <p> An aerial view of the Tracy Arm landslide and tsunami trimline captured during a US Geological Survey reconnaissance overflight on August 13 . <p> USGS <p> But those shrinking glaciers also draw tens of thousands of tourists to the state each year . " It 's because it just has n't happened to be above someone 's house or next to a cruise ship . " <p> The federal government and the state of Alaska are largely flying blind when it comes to tracking the landslides . <p> There is only one -- Barry Arm , 60 miles east of Anchorage on the Alaska coast -- that is continuously monitored by the US Geological Survey . Others in the area are checked periodically from satellites or aircraft . The Trump administration 's federal layoffs and budget cuts have winnowed the teams on the lookout , especially in Alaska 's heavily visited national parks . The Parks Service and USGS have been targeted for further steep layoffs by the Interior Department , according to court filings released this week . <p> The National Parks Service did n't respond to CNN 's questions about whether it informs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Cruise ships are docked in Juneau in 2016 . <p> Sergi Reboredo/VWPics/Redux <p> A crew member looks through binoculars on cruise ship Safari Endeavour in front of Margerie Glacier in Glacier Bay National Park . <p> Sergi Reboredo/VWPics/Redux <p> The landslide 's collapse at Tracy Arm was epic , but it was n't surprising to scientists . <p> A similar -- albeit smaller -- event happened just last year in Kenai Fjords National Park , when a landslide produced a 55-foot tsunami wave . @@130648903 <p> The Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters Database , which the Trump administration " retired " in May , has relaunched outside of the government using the same methodology . In its first update at the new site , the database shows that the first six months of 2025 have been the most expensive first six months of any year since 1980 . <p> The Billion-Dollar Database tracks the financial costs of property and other infrastructure destroyed by extreme weather disasters in the United States , focusing on events that caused $1 billion or more in damages . So far , 2025 has racked up $101.4 billion in such losses . The climate research nonprofit Climate Central now hosts the database and makes this information available to insurers , policy makers , broadcast meteorologists and ordinary citizens . <p> The database was rebuilt and will be maintained by its previous administrator Adam Smith , a former economist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration , the agency which used to host it . Smith found 14 billion-dollar disasters in the first half of this year , including the Los Angeles @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ US in mid-March.More billion-dollar disasters are likely to be added to the list before 2025 is over . <p> Without the database , the public would have no easy way to track the cost of extreme weather events , many of which are becoming more common and severe because of climate change . <p> But climate change is not the sole reason the database shows an upward trend in both the number of billion-dollar disasters and the amount they cost . Population growth and an increase in the number of buildings in harm 's way are the dominant factors , according to Smith . <p> " Either way you look at it , the rise in damages relates to human activities and choices , and so you need to use information in context to better evaluate future choices , " he said . <p> The frequency of billion-dollar disasters has particularly increased in the last decade , Smith said , occurring nearly twice as often compared to the 30-year inflation-adjusted average . <p> Between 1980 and 2024 , there were nine such disasters on average each year . In the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 24 . The record for a single year was 28 events in 2023 . <p> In the first six months of 2025 , the list of billion-dollar disasters is mostly comprised of severe thunderstorms and tornado outbreaks , reflecting the conspicuous absence of landfalling hurricanes so far this season . <p> However , the LA fires in January cost $61.2 billion , making them the costliest wildfires in US history , according to Climate Central . <p> Climate Central hired Smith after the NOAA economist took early retirement this year , as part of the Trump administration 's push to shrink the federal bureaucracy . <p> NOAA 's official list stopsat the end of2024 . Climate Central 's version picks up in 2025 and will continue from there . <p> The relaunched list uses the same methodology as the old NOAA one , Smith said . It relies on data from insurance companies and other sources , some of which is proprietary , to tally up total losses . The decision to discontinue the database was due in part to Smith 's exit from NOAA . It would have been @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , but it could have done it , he said . <p> The choice to discontinue the database was in keeping with the administration 's focus on cutting climate change datasets and programs across federal agencies . But there were calls for it to continue from multiple sectors . <p> " This dataset was simply too important to stop being updated . Demand for its revival actually came from several aspects of industry and society , including decision makers in the insurance , reinsurance risk space , academia , Congress and local communities , " Smith said .

Since 2022 , he 's been working on a new concept he calls " violent populism , " which he thinks could better represent the country 's current moment . He describes it as something " between civil war and nasty politics as usual . In addition , while both sides of the planet should be receiving and reflecting equal amounts of sunlight , the Earth 's Northern Hemisphere is reflecting less than the Southern Hemisphere , thus retaining more heat and appearing dimmer . <p> This affects the Earth 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the planet absorbs and re-emits into space as outgoing longwave radiation " , said Popular Mechanics . Oceans and weather systems link our continents and act as feedback @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ impacts ocean circulation and sea level rise and feeds into wave height and damage during storm events . We are losing species and habitats and our biodiversity is less intact and therefore less resilient . When biodiversity and ecosystems are less resilient to climate change , biodiversity loss is amplified . <p> Without international consensus on ways to limit emissions and protect biodiversity , these feedback loops will continue . The global risk management assessment by the Society of Actuaries and University of Exeter shows that we have massively underestimated climate change and nature driven risks . We have accepted much higher levels of risk than is broadly understood , or would be accepted if we did understand them . We are not calculating our risks adequately . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ budgets give a 50/50 chance of limiting warming to well below 2 ? C. The exact cost is extremely difficult to calculate . What is clear however is that while significant investment is required , payback on that investment will dwarf it . There are some clear investment wins in peatland restoration for example , but arguing about how much finance is needed is a distraction . It is a lot . @@130748345 <h> Why William Shakespeare was wrong about wildlife in the UK <p> This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today , and has been written by our American colleagues . It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald . <p> In the second act of Shakespeare 's A Midsummer Night 's Dream , Titania is sung to sleep by her fairies . Their lullaby begins : <p> You spotted snakes with double tongue , <p> Thorny hedgehogs , be not seen , <p> Newts and blindworms , do no wrong , <p> Come not near our Fairy Queen . <p> Titania is heading into a very hard night . She is , after all , on the point of being drugged by her estranged husband , leading to an infatuation with a donkey . However -- and far be it from me to question the bard -- I struggle with Shakespeare 's naked anti-wildlife propaganda . <p> Granted , in his day , spotted snakes AKA adders -- the UK 's only genuinely venomous terrestrial vertebrates -- would have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ land and field edges . Today they cling on as isolated populations on fragments of remnant habitat . The likelihood of an unfortunate encounter with a spotted snake , while still infinitesimally small , was hugely greater in the 1500s and 1600s . <p> An adder . ( Image : Danny Green ) <p> But were you a sleeping fairy , you would simply never have fallen foul of an adder . Adders strike humans ( and fairies ) exceptionally rarely and only in self-defence . In a lifetime of watching wildlife , I have known only two people bitten by adders . The first was a schoolfriend who stupidly picked up an infant adder while on a cross country run . Under the circumstances , the terrified viper can hardly be blamed for biting him . The second incident was likewise self-preservation . An ecologist friend , undertaking a reptile survey , mistakenly placed his hand a mere inch from a resting adder as he turned a tin sheet ( placed as a basking spot for reptiles and amphibians ) . Finding itself so close to a gigantic predator @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ its gorgeously patterned skin . My friend spent a night in hospital , with one hand worthy of Shrek , but suffered no long-term consequences . Adders want nothing more than to be left alone . <p> As for newts and blindworms , Shakespeare is -- as I believe he himself once said -- bang out of order . Newts are beautiful , peaceable creatures of ponds and pools . Shakespeare could learn a thing or two from P G Wodehouse 's Gussie Fink-Nottle who , though mocked by Bertie Wooster for his passion , displays a charming devotion to newts and their habits . Newts mean no harm , neither to humans nor to fairies . <p> Great crested newt ( Image : Kevin Caster ) <p> Shakespeare 's blindworms are what we would now term slow worms . They are not blind , nor indeed worms , nor are they remotely interested in harming Fairy Queens . Were a slow worm to cross paths with a slumbering fairy , it would most likely be hunting for slugs , worms or other invertebrates , and would pass her by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tongue . <p> I have recently had the privilege of contributing to planning for the forthcoming GCSE in natural history and let me tell you -- from this position of lofty authority -- that A Midsummer Night 's Dream might do very well as English Literature coursework ; but natural history , Shakespeare would likely fail . <p> And here 's the rub -- thank you Shakespeare for that bon mot -- the playwright 's greatest offence must surely be his casual hedgehog-bashing . Listen up , Shakey , you pick a fight with the prickly people and you pick a fight with me . <p> Hedgehogs , I ask you : those loveliest and most helpful of neighbours . What have hedgehogs done to you , Will ? I very much doubt they ever attacked , cursed or even startled your fairies . This said , I was once bitten on the ankle by a long-eared hedgehog in a ger tent in the Mongolian Gobi-Altai . The poor animal had been detained by local people the night before , had taken refuge in the skirts of the tent , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ singer . But I digress . <p> Were Shakespeare alive today , I like to think that he would twig how wrong he once was about hedgehogs , adders and newts . Being a sagacious sort , he would probably be a member of London Wildlife Trust ; perhaps , honouring his Stratford roots , a member of Warwickshire Wildlife Trust too . Certainly he 'd be a passionate advocate for hedgehogs . <p> For they -- and spotted snakes and blindworms -- have declined catastrophically since Shakespeare 's day and are still in steep decline today . While these species lead very different lives , it is -- irrefutably -- our human stranglehold on nature that has driven all of them from so many erstwhile haunts and so reduced their populations . <p> What these species need is simple . They need habitat : plenty of good habitat , which is undisturbed by humans , and by our dogs , cats , pheasants and other familiars . And untainted by the innumerable toxins with which we lace both land and water . This habitat must offer plenty of natural @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the case of hedgehogs , slow worms and adders -- somewhere safe to hibernate each winter . Crucially , these animals also need their habitats to be connected through living corridors across the landscape , for them to mingle genes , disperse , migrate and adapt to climate change . <p> Shakespeare made reference to adders , slow worms , newts and hedgehogs because these animals were relevant to his audience , known to them , loved by them , even in central London . Wonderful though they are , these are not mere interesting creatures . They are co-citizens of these islands , as native here as we are . They and their habitats should be known to everyone today , just as they were in Shakespeare 's life . It is our job -- at Norfolk Wildlife Trust , but just as much the job of everyone in society -- to re-imagine and recreate a landscape full of healthy habitat , in which all wild species can thrive again , can spread and multiply . <h> Useful Links <p> This website and associated newspapers adhere to the Independent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ If you have a complaint about the editorial content which relates to inaccuracy or intrusion , then please contact the editor here . @@130765977 <p> A thunderous boom follows a piercing crack , and we scramble to the sides of the boat , all eyes scanning the endless drift of icebergs , some shaped like a scoop of sorbet , others sheer-faced with sharp peaks . " When many icebergs are breaking , it means nice weather is coming . " Cruising among these icy giants shimmering in the sunshine , it sounds like credible wisdom . " You have to be able to talk to nature to survive up here , " Niels adds . <p> By " up here " , he is referring to Greenland , the world 's largest island and an autonomous , self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark that became a hot international topic earlier this year when President Trump suggested he would like to annex it . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , telling of characters who have long influenced Greenlandic culture -- and are experiencing a revival among younger generations curious about lost traditions . " We 're still learning , " Maria said . " We 're rediscovering our roots that were pulled up . " <p> Kayaking in Greenland with Intrepid Travel <p> Inuit communities have inhabited Greenland , or Kalaallit Nunaat in Greenlandic , for more than 4,500 years . The coming of Norse settlers in the 10th century , European whalers from the 17th century and then Danish-Norwegian ( later just Danish ) colonial rule from 1721 stripped away many indigenous traditions . This had an impact on everything from language to dress and customs such as tattooing -- all parts of Greenlandic heritage now being reclaimed . <p> Venturing north from Nuuk 's newly expanded airport , we flew to Ilulissat , Greenland 's third city , but really more of a port town . Situated around 180 miles into the Arctic Circle , Ilulissat -- which aptly translates to " Icebergs " -- sprawls over a rocky coastline where red , blue and yellow wooden-clad @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ than I had expected all punctuate the granite . While more than 5,000 people live here , it is the 3,000 Greenlandic sled dogs whose howls are the soundtrack to daily life . <p> In 2004 , the great tumbling mass of ice that is the Ilulissat Icefjord , known locally as Kangia , became a Unesco World Heritage Site , and in 2021 , the sweeping Icefjord Centre opened on this vast terrain . A marvel of wood and floor-to-ceiling glass panels , it takes you through " The Story of Ice " , from its formation and ecosystem to the impact of climate change . <p> From the centre , we clacked along the wooden walkway that protects the permafrost below , part of four waymarked hiking trails alongside the Icefjord . Rounding the rocky headland , we gasped at the craggy expanse of ice , dazzling in the sunshine , sandwiched between deep blue water and a pure blue sky . <p> We later found ourselves in Pauline Jensen 's snug home , where she hosts " kaffemik " , the Greenlandic tradition of feasting with friends @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ laden with fruit-stuffed buns , thickly buttered bread and bowls of freshly pressed apples and native crowberries gave a flavour of the sweet treats typically enjoyed alongside savoury dishes such as fish soup and reindeer stew during these social gatherings . <p> We sipped Labrador tea , infused with herbs of the same name , as Pauline told us that , " Family is perhaps the most important thing about Greenlandic culture . " And while she would love to see an independent Greenland , she appreciates the relationship with Denmark , and could n't foresee the situation changing to include another country -- at least not in her lifetime . <p> Homes in Nuuk City ( Photo : Arctic-Images/Getty ) <p> It 's a pertinent point . President Trump 's interest in Greenland has had some positive consequences . Bea Husum Terkildsen , destination manager at Visit Nuuk , told me , " all of a sudden we have some Danish politicians showing interest in improving things we 've been yelling about for decades " , such as local services , education and tourism . As a skipper on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ used to think about Greenland once every 10 years ; now it 's every week . " <p> Tourism is already on the up . In 2024 , Greenland saw the highest number of tourists ever recorded -- around 150,000 , with most concentrated around Ilulissat and the west coast -- and this is likely to rise further this year . Twenty-four-year-old Niels and his younger sister Anne Naduk Heilmann , whose family have been leading tours for many years , are helping to shape what comes next . <p> Another is 25-year-old guide Danny Molgaard , founder of local tour outfit Disko Adventures . I walked with him around Qeqertarsuaq -- Disko Island -- where houses , many without flushing loos , are dwarfed by icebergs in the bay . This is where he grew up , and he 's passionate about showcasing the landscapes to visitors . We zipped into drysuits and paddled alongside the icebergs , following Danny in kayaks under red basalt cliffs , black guillemots fluttering low across the swell . @@130778407 <h> How Melissa became a Category 5 monster <p> Tropical Storm Melissa took shape last Tuesday before rapidly strengthening as it moved west through the Caribbean . <p> A hurricane forms when warm , moist air rises from the ocean surface and creates a spinning system of clouds and storms . In the centre , air sinks , creating the eye , a calm , cloud-free zone surrounded by a wall of violent winds and rain known as the eye-wall . <p> Melissa 's origins trace back to a cluster of thunderstorms off the coast of West Africa in mid-October . By 21 October it had reached tropical storm strength and by 26 October , it was a Category 4 beast churning through the Caribbean Sea . <p> Ocean temperatures in the Caribbean are unusually high this year and hurricanes feed off that warm layer of water . Those conditions allowed Melissa to intensify quickly . <p> " The ocean is warmer and the atmosphere is warmer and moister because of climate change , " says Brian McNoldy , senior research associate at the University of Miami . <h> Low @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the strongest storms in the Atlantic this century . <p> For Jamaicans , the comparisons with past storms are chilling . If it strikes Jamaica at close to full strength , it could eclipse all the storms the island has experienced before . Gilbert in 1988 , the last direct hit , was a Category 3 . It destroyed thousands of homes and killed 49 people . Dean in 2007 and Beryl in 2024 came close , but neither matched Melissa 's power . <p> The storm 's central air pressure dropped to 892 millibars as of the National Hurricane Center 's advisory on Tuesday morning local time , below Hurricane Katrina 's 902 mb . The lower the pressure , the more violent the winds - making this one of the most powerful systems ever to form in the Atlantic . <p> Hurricane Katrina , which hit New Orleans in 2005 , killed 1,392 people and caused damage estimated at $125bn ( ? 94bn ) . <p> " This is going to be the strongest hurricane that 's ever hit Jamaica , at least in the records we have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at Oxford University 's Environmental Change Institute , told the BBC . <p> The storm has been blamed for four deaths in Haiti and the Dominican Republic . Jamaica 's minister of health said on Monday that three people had died on the island while preparing for the approaching storm . <p> Melissa strengthened particularly quickly , fuelled by very warm waters in the Caribbean , around one to two degrees above average . <p> " There has been a perfect storm of conditions leading to the colossal strength of Hurricane Melissa , " Dr Leanne Archer , research associate in climate extremes at the University of Bristol , said . <h> Slow pace poses catastrophic flooding risk <p> While the wind speed is staggeringly high , the storm 's movement is notably slow . Melissa itself was crawling westward at around 5km/h on Tuesday- slower than a person 's walking pace . <p> That lethargy , meteorologists warn , could be catastrophic as it means that a hurricane can bring rain to a single location for days on end , aggravating flooding . <p> When hurricanes stall , they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ leading to repeated waves of rain , flooding and wind damage . <p> One of the most famous examples of this is Hurricane Harvey in 2017 , which stalled over Houston in the US . Harvey released 100cm of rain in just three days , causing catastrophic flooding . <p> The US National Hurricane Center has warned that Jamaica could see 38 to 76 cm of rain , with as much as a metre in some mountainous areas . <p> Storm surges of up to four metres are possible , especially along the island 's southern and eastern shores . Low-lying parishes such as Clarendon and St Catherine are at risk of flash flooding not only from rainfall but also from torrents rushing down from the Blue Mountains . <p> " Imagine a metre of rainfall coming down in a whole basin and then being channelled down into a river network . That 's going to be metres and metres of flooding by the time it reaches the lower parts of that drainage network . So the flooding will probably result in a large loss of life , I imagine @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ year , said . <p> Image source , Reuters <p> Image caption , <p> As a low-lying island nation , it is particularly exposed to storms <p> Some research suggests hurricanes are generally moving more slowly than they used to . You could have your whole ground floor completely inundated @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " <p> In major cities like Kingston and Montego Bay , the construction is more robust , he said , but in rural and hillside areas , " there 's more vernacular architecture some things built from wood not the larger , concrete-type buildings " . Those will fare far worse . <p> " This hurricane will be very hard on Jamaica , " says Kerry Emanuel , professor emeritus of atmospheric science at Massachusetts Institute of Technology . <p> Jamaica is " unprepared to cope effectively " with major storms , Dr Patricia Green , an architect and preservationist based in Kingston told the BBC . She recalled how " a couple of hours of rainfall " in September caused " massive flooding " in the capital , exposing deep weaknesses in urban planning . <p> She criticised the surge of high-rise developments " sited in areas that should be the runoff of the city " , saying they had brought flooding to districts " that never had flooding before " . <p> As a low-lying island nation , it is particularly exposed to storms . These are not just in European countries such as Britain , France and Norway , but also French Polynesia and the Maldives , where sea level rise in the Indian Ocean nation now poses an existential threat . There is even a proposal for floating islands in the Baltic Sea on which small cities would be built . <p> Living on water is normal for us -- Marjan de Blok <p> A floating house can be constructed on any shoreline and is able to cope with rising seas or rain-induced floods by remaining atop the water 's surface . Unlike houseboats , which can easily be unmoored and relocated , floating homes are fixed to the shore , often resting on steel poles , and are usually connected to the local sewer system and power grid . They are structurally similar to houses built on land , but instead of a basement , they have a concrete hull that acts as a counterweight , allowing them to remain stable in the water . In the Netherlands , they are often prefabricated , square-shaped , three-storey townhouses built offsite with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ For cities facing worsening floods and a shortage of land for housing , floating homes are one potential blueprint to expand urban housing in the age of climate change . <p> Koen Olthuis , who in 2003 founded Waterstudio , a Dutch architectural firm focused exclusively on floating buildings , says the relatively lo-tech nature of floating homes is potentially their biggest advantage . The homes he designs are stabilised by poles dug roughly 65m ( 210ft ) into the ground and outfitted with shock-absorbent materials to reduce the feeling of movement from nearby waves . The houses ascend when waters rise and descend when waters recede . But despite their apparent simplicity , Olthuis contends they have the potential to transform cities in ways not seen since the introduction of the elevator , which pushed skylines upward . <p> Getty Images <p> The Netherlands is a pioneer for water-based developments , as a low-lying country that has had to work alongside the sea for centuries ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> " We now have the tech , the possibility to build on water , " says Olthuis @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ schools and health care centres . He added he and his colleagues " do n't see ourselves as architects , but as city doctors , and we see water as a medicine " . <p> In the Netherlands , a country which is largely built on reclaimed land and a third of which remains below sea level , the idea is not so far-fetched . In Amsterdam , which has almost 3,000 officially registered traditional houseboats across its canals , hundreds of people have moved into floating homes in previously neglected neighbourhoods . <p> Schoonschip , designed by Dutch firm Space&amp;Matter , consists of 30 houses , half of which are duplexes , on a canal in a former manufacturing area . The neighbourhood is a short ferry ride from central Amsterdam , where many of the residents work . Community members share nearly everything , including bikes , cars and food bought from local farmers . Each building runs its own heat pump and devotes roughly a third of its roof to greenery and solar panels . The 20-ish minutes until the missile is scheduled to hit its target are then replayed from three different perspectives , as we see officials at various levels of the US defensive infrastructure trying to figure out just what it is they could or should do to prevent and/or respond to such an attack . <p> Whereas Warfare immerses you wholeheartedly in a situation that , while viscerally horrific , is not one you 'd ever likely have to endure yourself unless you signed up to go to war , House of Dynamite portrays @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that we could be subject to , and would have absolutely no power to prevent . <p> That 's a stress with legs . You 'll be thinking about it long after watching , and you 'll also probably be thinking something along the lines of " What the fuck ? Could this actually happen ? Should I be worried about it all the time now ? Please help . " So we put all of our anxious thoughts to Sebastian Brixey-Williams , who 's the executive director of BASIC ( the British American Security Information Council ) , a think tank that works to reduce the risk that nuclear weapons pose to humanity . Are we all fucked ? Take it away , Sebastian . <p> Firstly , as someone who spends an awful lot of time thinking about nuclear weapons , what did you think of the film ? <p> I thought the film was great . It 's the film that the nuclear community has been waiting for -- one that actually shows real nuclear risks . There are a lot of films about using nuclear weapons @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as a plot device for terrorists , but there 's not much that looks at nuclear weapons in their native environment . So much attention goes to climate change , more recently AI . But it 's not like this problem has ever gone away , it 's just the political priorities have changed . Having the public engaged in this issue from a position of grounded realism , as opposed to the fantasy stories that often do happen around nuclear issues , is really important . <p> What do you think is the likelihood of a seemingly unprovoked attack like the one we see in the film ? <p> Typically , experts think about two kinds of scenario : the first is what they 'd call a limited nuclear use scenario , where you would have lower-yield nuclear weapons being used , maybe a small handful of them , in a localised environment . You might have a small exchange between India and Pakistan , for example , where they might attack only military assets on both sides . That kind of scenario , people assume would grow out @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ border conflict , for example . <p> Or , people worry about the other end of the scale , which is the sort of large-scale strategic thing : multiple cities on both sides , nuclear winter , all that kind of thing , and that is typically assumed to grow out of some kind of localised thing first . <p> People do n't tend to worry about the bolt from the blue , all-out Cold-War-style , " Are they going to just completely destroy the continent any second ? " , which was worried about for decades . There 's more political stability , arguably , but there 's also now the ability on both sides to respond to something like that , so it would be a self-defeating proposition . There 's also relative ease of identifying the culprit and so forth , so excluding that one , the other two are what people worry about . <p> So does the fact that the scenario in the film is n't really either of those mean it 's not very likely ? <p> Well , it 's not something that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ because it slightly mixes and matches between these two things that people worry about . So on the one hand , this is an attack on the US homeland , with what is assumed to be a large-yield nuclear weapon on a city . On the other hand , it 's not an all-out strike , it 's just this one-off . And so there 's very little work on this idea , and what 's interesting about the film is that they did n't spot exactly where it came from ; there was a cyberattack , which makes it difficult to identify who the culprit was . It 's incredibly difficult to comment on cyber operations versus nuclear because it 's so secretive , but it 's not outside the realms of possibility to imagine something like that happening . <p> On the other hand , even in the event that they actually do n't know who fired it in the first place , it 's obviously massively escalatory and one would assume it would n't happen on the basis that if the US were to find out who @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ seeing where the missile comes from is not the only way that you would do that -- the US response on whoever was responsible would be enormous . So the idea that it 's a deliberate attack , is , I think , difficult to believe , but it 's an interesting scenario and it 's not outside the realms of possibility . <p> It 's suggested in the film that it could be someone going rogue , or an accident -- I sort of assumed that there would be so many protocols , involving so many people , that neither of those is particularly likely . Is that right ? <p> It was certainly a concern in the Cold War , and in the Cuban Missile Crisis , the control over nuclear use was delegated down to the submarine level . You needed 3 on board to approve use , and there was this famous situation where Vasili Arkhipov was the one who held out and said no when the other two had approved it , so we were pretty close there . We talk about accidents and going @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be human . That 's probably the top three . And I say that because the situation was never stable , and it 's getting more and more unstable . This should be up there with climate change as a parallel existential threat that humanity faces on a daily basis . We 're moving from a situation in the Cold War where you had two superpowers who were essentially balanced to some extent -- which had major risks but a certain amount of stability as well -- through the unipolar moment where the US basically ran the world , to what 's happened in the last 10 years or more , of countries starting to challenge that dominance . The sustained -- and growing -- intensity of the storm is remarkable , experts say , and has the makings of a historic hurricane . <p> " When I look at the cloud pattern , I will tell you as a meteorologist and professional -- and a person -- it is beautiful , but it is terrifying , " says Sean Sublette , a meteorologist based in Virginia . Early Tuesday morning , as it approached Jamaica , Melissa was measuring a minimum pressure of 901 millibars ( mb ) -- lower than Hurricane Katrina 's peak low pressure of 902 mb @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ late in the year , according to Colorado State University meteorologist Philip Klotzbach . <p> Incredibly , as of Tuesday morning , Melissa was n't done intensifying .
